value: How do researchers perceive the progress, funding, job prospects, scientific rigor and leading theories of consciousness science relative to other neuroscience subfields?

Reports an informal online survey of 249 respondents showing that consciousness science is widely seen as making progress yet as harder to fund and to get a job in and as less rigorous than other neuroscience subfields, with the perceived rigor gap unrelated to the perceived funding and job difficulty, and with global workspace theory favoured overall but integrated information theory favoured by non-experts.

quote: Two hundred and fourty-nine subjects replied to our informal online survey.
The majority of respondents (78%) indicated that scientific research on consciousness has been making progress.

quote: The field of consciousness was seen as similarly or more rigorous than fields such as social neuroscience (33% reported consciousness science as “more rigorous” than social neuroscience, versus only 10% who reported it as “less rigorous”), again both by experts as well as non-experts.

value: Among non-experts the most promising theory was instead Integrated Information Theory at 22%, and this expert/non-expert split held under both definitions of expertise.

quote: FIGURE 1 | Responses to the question “Compared to some other subfields in neuroscience, how difficult is it to successfully compete for funding for doing empirical work on consciousness?” by primary region in which the respondents are based.
Two hundred and fourty-nine subjects replied to our informal online survey.
However, as can be seen in the data, e.g., Figure 3, a fairly broad group of experts were included in the survey (n = 106), in addition to a good number of non-experts (n = 143).
Overall, 80% of our participants were in academia.
On average, participants were 37 years old.
A great majority of participants (78%) agreed that progress has been made in the scientific study of consciousness.
More participants considered the work done in the field less rigorous than in other fields (34%), rather than the other way round (8%).
Overall, the global workspace theory (Dehaene and Changeux, 2011; Dehaene et al., 2014) was seen as the most promising theory of consciousness (28%).
This was especially true for participants based primarily in North America, compared to those based primarily in Europe [Wilcoxon ranksum test: p = 0.02].
We found no significant difference between experts and non-experts on the perceived difficulty of obtaining funding for studying consciousness [chi-squared test; p = 0.67].
This was especially true for participants based primarily in North America, compared to those based primarily in Europe [Wilcoxon ranksum test: p = 0.02].
This result appears to hold regardless of whether one studies consciousness or not, as we found no dependence between expertise and perceived progress in the field [chi-squared tests, p = 0.32].
